source.title: Some open problems in algebraic geometry and the Langlands program.

accepted.question_text: Given a target symmetry-bearing cohomological object, determine whether there exists an algebraic variety Y whose cohomology group H^i(Y), equipped with its natural symmetries, has the desired properties. In the background of this question is Grothendieck's idea that pieces of cohomology come from motives, so the problem is an inverse realization problem: starting from the properties one wants for a cohomology group or motivic piece, construct or prove the existence of a corresponding algebraic variety.

evidence.quote: But the problem often goes in the other direction : we look for an algebraic variety Y such that one of its cohomology groups Hᶦ(Y) (equipped with its symmetries) has some properties ... and we are not able to find Y, although we conjecture it exists.
Such parts of the cohomology groups Hᶦ(Y) come from mysterious objects, which Grothendieck called motives.

accepted.question_text: Establish the Langlands prediction that each spectral component of the space of automorphic forms for a global field F should admit an arithmetico-geometric interpretation as a motive, meaning a part of the cohomology of an algebraic variety over F. The slide states that this is far from proven in general: for number fields Shimura varieties give such an interpretation only under strong additional conditions, and for function fields Drinfeld shtuka varieties provide it at the cohomological level but not yet in a genuinely motivic way.

evidence.quote: Moreover each "color" of this decomposition (satisfying a condition in the case of number fields) should have an arithmetico-geometric interpretation ; namely, it should be a motive, i.e. a "part of the cohomology" of an algebraic variety Y over F.
This is far from being proven in general :
- in the case of function fields, varieties of Drinfeld shtukas (introduced in the 70s) give the answer in general, at the level of cohomology, but unfortunately not yet in a motivic way.

accepted.question_text: Understand the multiplicities that occur in the spectral decomposition predicted by the Langlands program. More precisely, beyond merely decomposing automorphic forms into spectral pieces, determine how multiplicities should be described and computed within that conjectural decomposition.

evidence.quote: 1) We want also to understand multiplicities in the spectral decomposition conjectured by the Langlands program.
Major works were done by Arthur and Ngo Bao Chau. In the easier case of function fields, Alain Genestier and I have a project about this question.

accepted.question_text: Prove and conceptualize Langlands' functoriality conjecture. In the wording of the slide, this conjecture is viewed as a quantization problem, so the open problem is not only to establish the transfers predicted by functoriality but to understand them through a mechanism analogous to quantization, the passage from classical mechanics to quantum mechanics.

evidence.quote: 2) Another conjecture of Langlands, called the "functoriality conjecture", is very important.
I like to see it as a quantization problem. Quantization is the way we pass from classical mechanics to quantum mechanics, it is always a mystery.

accepted.question_text: Prove the Riemann hypothesis together with its modern generalizations involving automorphic forms. As framed on the slide, the open problem encompasses both the classical Riemann hypothesis and the broader automorphic analogues that extend it beyond the function-field cases proved by Deligne.

evidence.quote: 3) The Riemann hypothesis (together with its modern generalizations which involve automorphic forms) is the biggest problem in mathematics.
The analogues of the Riemann hypothesis for function fields were proven by Deligne in the 70s.
